abstract.t: This document defines the WTX-1 (WaiTag Transfer Protocol, version 1) for preserving pseudonymous user context across unrelated web domains without third-party cookies, browser fingerprinting, login requirements, or personal data collection. The protocol uses cryptographically generated pseudonymous identifiers (WaiTags), URL hash fragment transport with early-cleanup scripts, server-side verification with replay protection, and DNS-based domain authorization to enable privacy-respecting cross-domain analytics.

This revision (draft-01) adds early-cleanup script specification, replay protection with nonce tracking, a complete threat model with browser extension analysis, measurable security properties with quantifiable claims, and expanded privacy considerations. The document is positioned as a research contribution on privacy-preserving cross-domain identity relevant to the IRTF Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group (PEARG).

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Third-party cookies have been the primary mechanism for cross-domain user identification since the 1990s. With Safari's Intelligent Tracking Prevention (ITP) deployed in 2017, Firefox Enhanced Tracking Protection (ETP) in 2019, and Chrome's Privacy Sandbox initiative beginning in 2024, this mechanism is being eliminated across all major browsers.

When a user navigates from one domain to an unrelated domain (different effective top-level domain plus one label, or eTLD+1), analytics systems lose the ability to understand that the same visitor made both visits. This creates blind spots in patient journey analytics across healthcare providers, financial customer experience across banking portals, government service usage across agency domains, and multi-brand retail analytics.
WTX-1 addresses these limitations by defining a protocol that:

ol.li: Preserves visitor context across unrelated domains
Never collects, transmits, or derives personal information
Works without cookies, fingerprinting, or login
Resists tracking by unauthorized third parties via DNS-based domain authorization
Degrades gracefully when consent is denied
Operates within GDPR, CCPA, and ePrivacy frameworks

section.t: This document presents WTX-1 as a research contribution to the study of privacy-preserving cross-domain identity mechanisms. The protocol is relevant to the IRTF Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group (PEARG), whose charter includes "privacy analysis of proposed and deployed technologies." WTX-1 provides measurable security properties (Section 13) that can be independently verified, enabling rigorous privacy analysis by the research community.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Changes from draft-00
section.t: This revision includes the following changes:

ul.li: Added early-cleanup script specification (Section 5.2)
Changed query parameter transport to opt-in only (Section 5.3)
Added replay protection as a MUST requirement (Section 6.2)
Added nonce field to token format for replay protection
Added complete threat model and mitigations (Section 9)
Added browser extension limitation analysis (Section 9.3)
Added measurable security properties (Section 13)
Expanded privacy considerations (Section 12)
Added PEARG-relevant framing for research community engagement
Added Performance API and PEARG charter references
Updated WaiTag entropy from 64 bits to 128 bits

dl.dd: A pseudonymous identifier generated per-visitor using cryptographic randomness. Format: wai_<random>_<domain_hash>. Contains no personally identifiable information (PII).
The domain where the user's session begins and the WaiTag is generated.
The domain the user navigates to, which receives and verifies the WaiTag via a cross-domain token.
A time-limited, server-signed token encoding the WaiTag for transfer between domains.
Domain ownership verification via DNS TXT records that authorizes a domain to participate in WTX-1 identity sharing.
The server-side component that issues, signs, and verifies cross-domain tokens.
A degraded operating mode where no WaiTag is generated, no identity is preserved, and identity-related API calls are no-ops.
An inline <head> script that strips tokens from the URL before any other scripts execute, minimizing the token visibility window.

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: The WTX-1 protocol operates across three participants: the origin domain, the destination domain, and the verification server.

figure.name: WTX-1 Protocol Flow
figure.artwork: Domain A Verification Domain B (Origin) Server (Destination) | | | 1. User visits | | 2. Generate WaiTag | | 3. Register WaiTag ---->| | | 4. Store WaiTag | | | | 5. User clicks link | | to Domain B | | 6. Request token ------>| | | 7. Verify DNS | | authorization | |<--------- 8. Return signed token | | | | 9. Append token to | | URL hash fragment | | | | | |--- User navigates to Domain B ----------->| | | | | | 10. Early-cleanup | | | script strips | | | token from URL | | | | | | 11. SDK reads token | | | from stashed var| | |<---- 12. Verify token | | | | | 13. Check signature, | | expiry, domain, | | replay (nonce) | | | | | |----> 14. Return | | | identity | | | | | | 15. Restore WaiTag | | | Clean URL |

ol.li: WaiTag Generation: When a user first visits a participating domain, the client generates a WaiTag using the Web Crypto API (crypto.getRandomValues). The WaiTag format is wai_<random_id><domain_hash>.
Identity Registration: The client registers the WaiTag with the verification server. The server stores the WaiTag, session ID, originating domain, and timestamp.

Cross-Domain Navigation: When the user navigates to another participating domain, a cross-domain token is appended to the destination URL. The mechanism for link decoration is implementation-defined (e.g., server-side link rewriting, client-side click handlers, or manual URL construction).

Token Generation: The verification server generates a signed, time-limited token encoding the user's WaiTag and session context. The server SHOULD verify that the destination domain is DNS-authorized before issuing the token.

Hash Fragment Transport: The token is appended to the destination URL as a hash fragment (#nylo_token=<token>). Hash fragments are never sent to the server in HTTP requests, providing an additional privacy layer.

Early Cleanup: On the destination domain, an inline <head> script executes before any other scripts, reads the token from the hash fragment, stashes it in a short-lived JavaScript variable (window.__nylo_early_token), and immediately cleans the URL using history.replaceState(). This ensures the token is never visible to third-party page scripts.

Token Verification: The SDK reads the token from the stashed variable (or from the hash fragment as fallback if the early-cleanup script is not deployed), and sends it to the verification server for validation.

Identity Restoration: If verification succeeds (signature valid, not expired, domain authorized, not previously used), the server returns the original WaiTag and session context. The client restores the user's pseudonymous identity on the new domain.

section.name: Structure
section.t: A WaiTag has the following structure:
The random component provides 128 bits of cryptographic entropy (16 bytes from the Web Crypto API), encoded in base-36 for compactness.

section.name: Properties
section.t: A WaiTag has the following properties:

ul.li: Not reversible: No component can be reversed to identify a natural person.
Not derived from PII: No personal information is used as input.
Domain-scoped: The domain hash binds the WaiTag to its origin, but the hash is one-way and cannot reveal the domain to a third party.
Collision-resistant: 128 bits of cryptographic randomness provides sufficient uniqueness for analytics use cases. For 1 billion identifiers, the collision probability is approximately 1.47 x 10^-21.
Not a fingerprint: No hardware, software, or behavioral signals are used.
Not deterministic: The same user on the same device will receive different WaiTags across sessions unless identity is explicitly restored via cross-domain token.

section.name: Generation Requirements
section.t: Implementations MUST generate WaiTags using crypto.getRandomValues or an equivalent cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG). If the Web Crypto API is not available, implementations MAY fall back to Math.random, but SHOULD log a warning indicating reduced randomness quality.

section.name: Primary: URL Hash Fragment
section.t: The cross-domain token MUST be transported via URL hash fragment as the primary mechanism:
Hash fragments (the portion of a URL after "#") are processed entirely client-side per Section 3.5. They are:

ul.li: Never included in HTTP requests to the server
Never logged in server access logs
Never sent in the Referer header
Not visible to network intermediaries (proxies, CDNs, WAFs)

section.t: This provides a stronger privacy guarantee than URL query parameters, which are transmitted to the server and commonly logged.

section.name: Early-Cleanup Script
section.t: To minimize the token visibility window, implementations SHOULD deploy an inline early-cleanup script in the <head> of every destination page. This script MUST execute before any other scripts (including third-party analytics, tag managers, and ad scripts).
Behavior:

ol.li: The script reads the URL hash fragment.
If a nylo_token or wai_token parameter is present, the script extracts the token value.
The token is stored in a short-lived JavaScript variable (window.__nylo_early_token).
Timing data is captured via performance.now() and stored in window.__nylo_early_token_timing.
The token is immediately removed from the URL using history.replaceState().
Any remaining non-token hash parameters are preserved.

section.t: Reference implementation:
section.sourcecode:
<script>
(function(){
  try{
    var s=performance.now();
    var h=window.location.hash;
    if(h&&(h.indexOf("nylo_token=")>-1||h.indexOf("wai_token=")>-1)){
      var p=new URLSearchParams(h.substring(1));
      var t=p.get("nylo_token")||p.get("wai_token");
      if(t){
        window.__nylo_early_token=t;
        p.delete("nylo_token");p.delete("wai_token");
        var n=p.toString();
        history.replaceState(null,"",
          window.location.pathname+window.location.search+(n?"#"+n:""));
        var e=performance.now();
        window.__nylo_early_token_timing={
          start:s,cleaned:e,duration:e-s
        };
      }
    }
  }catch(e){}
})();
</script>
section.t: Placement requirements:

ul.li: MUST be placed inline in the <head> element.
MUST appear before any <script src="..."> tags (including analytics, tag managers, and the SDK itself).
MUST NOT be loaded asynchronously or deferred.
SHOULD be the first <script> element in the document.

section.t: Without the early-cleanup script, the token remains in the URL hash from the moment the page starts loading until the SDK initializes and cleans it. During this window, any JavaScript on the page — including third-party scripts — can read window.location.hash and see the token. The early-cleanup script removes the token from the URL before other scripts execute.

The early-cleanup script stashes the token in window.__nylo_early_token, which is a globally accessible JavaScript variable. Any script that runs after the early-cleanup script and knows this variable name can read the token. This is a deliberate trade-off: the token must be stored somewhere between early-cleanup and SDK initialization. However, this is significantly more secure than leaving the token in the URL hash because window.location.hash is a well-known, commonly inspected property, while window.__nylo_early_token is an implementation-specific variable that third-party scripts have no reason to look for. The SDK deletes this variable immediately upon consuming it.

section.name: Opt-In Fallback: URL Query Parameters
section.t: Query parameter token transport is disabled by default. If hash fragment transport is not feasible (e.g., the destination URL uses hash-based client-side routing that would conflict with the token), the implementation MAY explicitly opt in to search parameter transport:
Privacy implications of query parameter transport:

ul.li: Query parameters ARE included in HTTP requests to the destination server.
Query parameters ARE logged in server access logs by default.
Query parameters MAY appear in Referer headers sent to third parties.
Query parameters ARE visible to network intermediaries.

section.t: Implementations using query parameter transport MUST remove the token from the URL immediately after reading it, using the History API (history.replaceState) to clean the URL without triggering a page reload. Implementations SHOULD also implement server-side log redaction and configure Referrer-Policy: no-referrer or same-origin headers.

section.name: Parameter Names
section.t: Implementations MUST accept both of the following parameter names for cross-domain tokens:

ul.li: "nylo_token" (primary)
"wai_token" (legacy/alternative)

section.name: Token Cleanup
section.t: Token cleanup operates in two phases:

Phase 1 (Early Cleanup, recommended): The inline <head> early-cleanup script (Section 5.2) strips the token from the URL hash fragment before any other scripts execute. The token is stashed in window.__nylo_early_token for the SDK to consume.

Phase 2 (SDK Cleanup, fallback): If the early-cleanup script is not deployed, the SDK MUST remove the token from the URL when it initializes. This cleanup occurs later in the page lifecycle, so a brief visibility window exists between page load and SDK initialization.
After reading the cross-domain token, the client MUST:

ul.li: Remove the token from the URL via history.replaceState()
Delete window.__nylo_early_token if it was used
Preserve any non-token hash parameters or search parameters

section.t: Token cleanup prevents:

ul.li: Accidental sharing of token-bearing URLs
Token replay from browser history
Token exposure in analytics tools that capture full URLs

section.name: Token Contents
section.t: A cross-domain token encodes the following fields:

tr.td: The session identifier from the origin domain
The domain that issued the token
Unique per-token identifier for replay protection

section.t: The token encoding format is implementation-defined. Common choices include JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and opaque server-side tokens with a lookup key.

section.name: Verification Requirements
section.t: The verification server MUST check:

ol.li: Signature validity: The token has not been tampered with.
Expiry: The token has not expired. The expiry window is configurable; the recommended default is 5 minutes (300 seconds).
Replay protection: The token has not been previously verified. Each token MUST only be accepted once. The server MUST maintain a record of consumed token nonces for at least the token expiry window.

section.t: The verification server SHOULD also check:

ol.li: Domain authorization: The destination domain is DNS-authorized to receive identities.
Origin matching: The token was issued for the domain making the verification request.

section.t: Error codes:

tr.td: Token has passed its expiry timestamp
Token has already been verified (replay attempt)
Token origin does not match the requesting domain's referrer

section.name: Verification Endpoint
section.t: The verification endpoint accepts a POST request with Content-Type application/json containing the token, the requesting domain, a customer identifier, and the HTTP Referer value.
Request body:
Success response:
Failure response:

section.name: Purpose
section.t: Before a domain can receive cross-domain identities, it SHOULD prove ownership via a DNS TXT record. This prevents unauthorized domains from requesting or receiving WaiTags and ensures that only domains controlled by the same organization (or participating partners) can share visitor context.

section.name: TXT Record Format
section.t: The DNS TXT record uses the following format:
The verification code is a unique value generated by the verification server for each domain registration.

ol.li: The domain owner registers the domain with the verification server and receives a verification code.
The domain owner adds the TXT record to their DNS configuration.
The domain owner calls the verification endpoint.
The server performs a DNS lookup for _nylo-verify.<domain>.
If the TXT record matches the expected verification code, the domain is authorized.
Authorization is cached server-side and periodically re-verified.

section.name: Subdomain Inheritance
section.t: If a parent domain (e.g., example.com) is DNS-verified, subdomains (e.g., blog.example.com, shop.example.com) inherit authorization automatically. Implementations MAY provide configuration to exclude specific subdomains from inheritance.

section.name: Three-Layer Strategy
section.t: The client SHOULD store identity data using multiple mechanisms for resilience against browser storage restrictions. These storage mechanisms are used exclusively for local identity persistence on a single domain — they are never used for cross-domain token transport (which uses URL hash fragments as defined in Section 5).

section.name: Storage Read Priority
section.t: When restoring identity, the client reads in order: cookie, localStorage, sessionStorage. The first valid result is used.

section.name: Data Stored
section.t: The stored identity record contains:
The "integrity" field is a one-way hash of the session ID, domain, WaiTag, and customer ID, used to detect tampering.

section.name: Data Obfuscation
section.t: Data stored in localStorage SHOULD be encoded with a customer-specific salt and timestamp to prevent casual inspection. This is obfuscation, not cryptographic security. The stored data contains no PII regardless of encoding.

section.name: Consent API
section.t: Implementations MUST provide a consent API that integrates with Consent Management Platforms (CMPs). The API MUST support the following operations:

ul.li: setConsent({analytics: false}) - Deny consent, switch to anonymous mode
setConsent({analytics: true}) - Grant consent, restore identity tracking
getConsent() - Query current consent state, returns {analytics: boolean}

section.name: Anonymous Mode Behavior
section.t: When consent is denied, the client MUST operate in anonymous mode with the following behavior:

ul.li: Event tracking remains active but with no identity attached.
WaiTag generation is disabled; waiTag is null.
The identify() API call is a no-op and is silently ignored.
getSession() returns null for waiTag and userId fields.
Cross-domain identity is disabled; no tokens are generated or accepted.
Only a session-scoped anonymous identifier is used (format: anon_<timestamp>_<random>).
No persistent identity data is written to cookies, localStorage, or sessionStorage.

section.name: Consent Restoration
section.t: When consent is granted after starting in anonymous mode:

ol.li: The client checks for previously stored identity data.
If found, the existing WaiTag and session are restored.
If not found, a new WaiTag is generated.
Cross-domain token checking is activated.
Full identity tracking resumes.

section.name: Regulatory Considerations
section.t: WaiTags are designed to fall outside the GDPR definition of "personal data" as defined in Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 because they contain no information derived from a natural person, cannot be reversed or cross-referenced to identify someone, and are not deterministic across sessions.

However, the classification of pseudonymous identifiers under data protection law varies by jurisdiction and is subject to evolving regulatory interpretation. Implementers SHOULD consult local legal counsel. The anonymous mode provides a conservative fallback for jurisdictions where pseudonymous identifiers may be considered personal data.

tr.td: Token interception by third-party page scripts

section.name: Early-Cleanup Script: Defense in Depth
section.t: The early-cleanup script (Section 5.2) is the primary defense against token exposure to unauthorized JavaScript. The execution timeline shows what each actor can see at each stage of page load:
section.artwork:
Timeline: Page Load with Cross-Domain Token
t0: Browser receives HTML response URL bar shows: destination.com/page#nylo_token=eyJ3... No scripts have executed yet.
t1: Early-cleanup <head> script executes (synchronous) 1. Reads window.location.hash 2. Extracts token -> window.__nylo_early_token 3. Calls history.replaceState() to clean URL URL bar now shows: destination.com/page Duration: < 1ms
t2: Other <head> scripts execute (tag managers, analytics) window.location.hash is EMPTY These scripts cannot see the token in the URL. window.__nylo_early_token exists but is an implementation-specific variable.
t3: DOM begins rendering URL bar is clean. User never sees the token.
t4: SDK initializes 1. Reads window.__nylo_early_token 2. Deletes window.__nylo_early_token 3. Sends token to verification server 4. Server checks: signature, expiry, replay, domain 5. Identity restored
t5: Token fully consumed Token no longer exists anywhere on the page: - Not in URL bar - Not in window.__nylo_early_token - Not in browser history (replaceState) - Invalidated server-side (one-time-use)

section.name: Browser Extension Limitation Analysis
section.t: Browser extensions represent the one token interception vector that cannot be fully mitigated at the application layer.

Browser extensions with content script access can declare "run_at": "document_start" in their manifest. This tells the browser to inject the extension's content script before the page's own <head> scripts execute. At this point, the extension has access to window.location.hash, which still contains the token. This is by design — it is how the browser extension model works.
Despite extensions having theoretical access, the practical risk is low:

ol.li: Extensions must be explicitly installed by the user. A malicious extension would need to pass marketplace review, be discovered by the target user, and specifically target WTX-1 tokens.
Tokens are one-time-use. The extension must race to verify the token before the SDK does. If the extension wins, the SDK verification fails and no identity is restored — no data is compromised.
Tokens expire in 5 minutes. A captured token cannot be stored for later use.
Tokens contain only pseudonymous data. Even if intercepted, no real person is identified.
The user whose token is intercepted is the same user who installed the extension.

section.t: This limitation is not unique to WTX-1. OAuth 2.0 redirect tokens, SAML assertions, JWTs in localStorage, and session cookies are all accessible to browser extensions. WTX-1's one-time-use and short expiry model provides stronger protection against extension interception than most alternatives.

The only way to fully eliminate extension access would be a browser-native API that mediates token transport without exposing the token to any JavaScript. If WTX-1 gains adoption, this analysis can serve as the basis for proposing such an API to the W3C.

section.name: HTTPS Requirement
section.t: All token transport and verification MUST occur over HTTPS. The protocol MUST NOT be used over unencrypted HTTP.

section.name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
section.t: If the destination page is vulnerable to XSS, an attacker's injected script could read the hash fragment or window.__nylo_early_token before the SDK consumes it. Implementations MUST sanitize all token data before use and never insert token values into the DOM without proper escaping. The early-cleanup script mitigates this partially by reducing the window, but an XSS vulnerability undermines all client-side security guarantees.

section.name: DNS Spoofing
section.t: DNS TXT record verification is subject to DNS spoofing attacks. Implementations SHOULD use DNSSEC where available and validate DNS responses over secure channels (DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS).

section.name: Server-Side Key Management
section.t: The shared HMAC key used for token signing MUST be stored securely. Implementations SHOULD rotate HMAC keys periodically (recommended: every 90 days), support multiple active keys during rotation periods, and use hardware security modules (HSMs) or key management services where available.

section.name: Rate Limiting
section.t: Verification endpoints MUST implement rate limiting to prevent token brute-force attacks, denial-of-service, and nonce table exhaustion. Recommended limits: 100 verification requests per IP per minute, with exponential backoff on failures.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The complete threat model and mitigations are described in Section 9. This section summarizes the key security requirements.

ul.li: Tokens MUST be signed server-side using HMAC or an equivalent mechanism.
Tokens MUST have a configurable expiry window. The recommended default is 5 minutes.
Tokens MUST be single-use. The server MUST reject replayed tokens with TOKEN_REPLAYED.
Token verification MUST validate the signature, expiry, and replay status.
All API communication between the client and the verification server MUST use HTTPS .
Hash fragment transport prevents server-side token logging by design, as fragments are not included in HTTP requests per .
Query parameter transport is disabled by default and requires explicit opt-in.
The early-cleanup script (Section 5.2) SHOULD be deployed to minimize the token visibility window.
All client-supplied strings MUST be sanitized to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. HTML entity encoding is RECOMMENDED.
String fields MUST be length-limited. The recommended maximum is 1,000 characters.
Domain values MUST be validated before use in DNS lookups or token generation.
API endpoints MUST implement rate limiting. The recommended default is 100 requests per IP address per minute.
Rate limit status MUST be communicated via X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset response headers.
Exceeded limits MUST return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests).

section.name: Response Headers
section.t: Servers implementing WTX-1 SHOULD set the following security-related response headers:

ul.li: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()
Content-Security-Policy: Appropriate policy for the deployment
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains (when serving over HTTPS)

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions.
If this protocol achieves broader adoption, the following registrations may be requested in future revisions:

ul.li: Registration of the "_nylo-verify" DNS underscore name prefix in the "Underscored and Globally Scoped DNS Node Names" registry per RFC 8552.
Registration of the "nylo_token" and "wai_token" URI fragment parameter names if a suitable registry is established.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: WTX-1 is designed from the ground up to preserve user privacy while enabling cross-domain analytics. This section details the privacy properties, guarantees, and limitations of the protocol. This analysis is relevant to the IRTF PEARG charter on "privacy analysis of proposed and deployed technologies."

ol.li: No PII collection: The protocol never collects, transmits, or derives personal information such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, or physical addresses.
No fingerprinting: No hardware, software, or behavioral signals (screen resolution, installed fonts, GPU rendering, etc.) are used to generate or correlate identifiers.
No third-party cookies: Cross-domain identity does not use the Set-Cookie/Cookie HTTP mechanism for cross-domain transfer.
No login required: Identity preservation works for anonymous visitors without requiring authentication or account creation.
Consent-respecting: The protocol degrades to fully anonymous tracking when consent is denied, ensuring compliance with opt-out requirements.
Domain-authorized: Only DNS-verified domains can participate in identity sharing, preventing unauthorized cross-domain tracking.
Time-limited tokens: Cross-domain tokens expire (default 5 minutes), preventing indefinite tracking or token reuse.
Client-side token reading: Hash fragment transport ensures tokens are never sent to destination servers in HTTP requests.

section.name: Pseudonymous Identifiers and GDPR
section.t: WaiTags are pseudonymous identifiers generated using cryptographically secure random number generators (window.crypto.getRandomValues). They contain no embedded personal information, device characteristics, or derivable real-world identity. A WaiTag cannot be reversed to identify a natural person without access to a separate mapping table, which the protocol does not define or require.

Under GDPR, pseudonymous identifiers are considered personal data when they can be attributed to a natural person using additional information (Article 4(5)). WTX-1 does not define or require such a mapping. Implementors who create such mappings take on the full obligations of a GDPR data controller.
Implementors SHOULD NOT create WaiTag-to-identity mappings unless they have a clear lawful basis and have completed a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

section.name: User Control and Consent
section.t: Implementations MUST provide users with clear mechanisms to:

ol.li: Opt out of cross-domain identity sharing while retaining single-domain analytics.
Clear their WaiTag and session data at any time.
View what data has been collected about their pseudonymous identity.
Request deletion of all data associated with their WaiTag (GDPR Article 17).

section.t: When a user denies consent, the protocol MUST degrade gracefully to anonymous mode where no cross-domain tokens are generated or accepted, and only aggregate, non-identifiable analytics are collected.

section.name: Data Minimization
section.t: The protocol follows the principle of data minimization as required by GDPR Article 5(1)(c). Cross-domain tokens contain only the minimum fields necessary for identity verification. No behavioral data, page content, interaction history, device information, or browsing history is included in the token.

section.name: Cross-Domain Tracking Scope
section.t: Cross-domain identity sharing is limited to domains that have been explicitly authorized via DNS TXT records. This prevents a domain from being included in a tracking network without the domain owner's explicit consent.
Implementations MUST NOT allow wildcard domain authorization or open enrollment of domains into a tracking network.

section.name: Consent-Gated Degradation
section.t: When consent is denied:

ul.li: No WaiTag is generated or stored
No cross-domain tokens are created or accepted
Events are tracked with a random per-session identifier only
No data persists beyond the current page session
The SDK operates in a fully anonymous mode with no cross-domain capability

section.name: Identifier Rotation
section.t: WaiTags stored in localStorage persist until explicitly cleared. To limit the window of potential correlation, implementations SHOULD implement rotation policies — for example, regenerating the WaiTag every 90 days. This bounds the maximum duration over which a single pseudonymous identifier can be used to correlate cross-domain visits.

section.name: Regulatory Compliance
section.t: WTX-1 is designed to operate within the following regulatory frameworks:

ul.li: GDPR (EU): Pseudonymous processing with data minimization, purpose limitation, and right to erasure support.
CCPA/CPRA (California): No sale of personal information; supports opt-out mechanisms.
ePrivacy Directive (EU): No use of cookies or similar technologies for cross-domain transfer; hash fragment transport does not trigger cookie consent requirements.
HIPAA (US Healthcare): No collection or transmission of Protected Health Information (PHI).
COPPA (US Children): Protocol does not collect age information; implementors in child-directed services MUST implement additional safeguards.

section.name: Limitations and Residual Risks
section.t: While WTX-1 provides strong privacy guarantees, the following residual risks should be acknowledged:

ul.li: Server-side correlation: Organizations operating multiple domains may correlate WaiTags server-side. The protocol limits this to DNS-authorized domains but cannot prevent the authorizing organization from performing correlation.
Token interception: Although hash fragment transport prevents tokens from being sent in HTTP requests, tokens may be visible to browser extensions or client-side JavaScript before cleanup occurs.
Referrer leakage: Some browsers may include hash fragments in Referer headers under certain conditions. Implementations SHOULD set Referrer-Policy headers.
Long-lived sessions: If WaiTags are stored without expiration, they persist indefinitely. Implementations SHOULD implement rotation or expiration policies.

section.name: Research Questions for Privacy Analysis
section.t: The following open questions are relevant to the PEARG research community and are offered for analysis and discussion:

ol.li: Is hash fragment transport a sufficient privacy boundary, or should browser APIs provide a dedicated secure channel for cross-domain context transfer?
What is the appropriate entropy threshold for pseudonymous identifiers to balance collision resistance with correlation risk?
How does DNS-based domain authorization compare to other trust establishment mechanisms (e.g., certificate-based, blockchain-based) for preventing unauthorized tracking network expansion?
Can the early-cleanup script's effectiveness be formally verified against the browser execution model, or are there edge cases where script execution order is not guaranteed?
What rotation period for pseudonymous identifiers optimally balances analytics utility with privacy protection?

section.name: Measurable Security Properties
section.t: This section defines quantifiable security claims that can be independently verified through measurement. Each claim includes its expected value, measurement methodology, and (where applicable) the SDK API for programmatic verification. These measurable properties are central to PEARG-style privacy analysis, enabling reproducible evaluation of the protocol's security guarantees.

section.name: Logging Surface Reduction
section.t: Claim: When using hash fragment transport (default), cross-domain tokens appear in 0 out of 6 standard HTTP logging fields.

table.name: Token Presence in HTTP Logging Fields

section.t: Measurement methodology: Configure a destination server to log all request headers and the full request URI. Navigate to destination.com/page#nylo_token=test_token. Verify that test_token does not appear in any server-side log entry. Repeat with destination.com/page?nylo_token=test_token and verify it appears in all 6 fields.
SDK verification: The SDK exposes getTimingMetrics().loggingSurfaceFields which returns 0 for hash transport and 6 for query transport.

section.name: Token Visibility Window
section.t: Claim: With the early-cleanup script deployed, the token is visible in window.location.hash for less than 1 millisecond. Without early-cleanup, the token is visible for the entire duration from page load to SDK initialization (typically 200-800ms depending on page complexity).

Measurement methodology: The early-cleanup script captures performance.now() timestamps at script start, token extraction, and URL cleanup (history.replaceState). The visibility window is the duration between start and cleanup completion. These timestamps are stored in window.__nylo_early_token_timing and consumed by the SDK.
SDK verification: getTimingMetrics().earlyCleanup.durationMs reports the early-cleanup duration. getTimingMetrics().tokenVisibilityWindowMs reports the total visibility window.

section.name: Token Entropy
section.t: Claim: Each WaiTag contains 128 bits of cryptographic entropy from the Web Crypto API .

Measurement methodology: Generate 10,000 WaiTags and verify no collisions. Extract the random component and verify uniform distribution across the base-36 character space. Verify the source is crypto.getRandomValues (not Math.random).
Expected collision probability: For 128 bits of entropy, the probability of collision in a set of N identifiers is approximately N^2 / 2^129. For 1 billion identifiers: approximately 1.47 x 10^-21.

section.name: Token Lifetime and Replay Surface
section.t: Claim: Each token is valid for exactly one verification attempt and expires after a configurable window (default: 300 seconds / 5 minutes).

Measurement methodology: Generate a cross-domain token. Submit it for verification — expect success. Submit the same token again — expect TOKEN_REPLAYED error. Generate a new token, wait more than 300 seconds, submit — expect TOKEN_EXPIRED error.

section.name: Token Verification Latency
section.t: Claim: End-to-end token verification (from SDK token detection to server response) completes in under 100ms on typical network conditions.
SDK verification: getTimingMetrics().tokenVerification.durationMs reports the verification round-trip duration. getTimingMetrics().sdkInitDurationMs reports total SDK initialization time.

section.name: HTTP Data Leakage
section.t: Claim: With hash fragment transport, exactly 0 bytes of token data are transmitted in any HTTP request from the client to the destination server.

This is a structural guarantee, not a runtime measurement. Per Section 3.5, the fragment component of a URI is not sent in HTTP requests. This behavior is implemented by all conforming HTTP user agents and cannot be overridden by JavaScript or server configuration.

Measurement methodology: Set up a packet capture (tcpdump/Wireshark) on the destination server. Navigate to destination.com/page#nylo_token=test_value. Inspect the HTTP GET request — verify test_value does not appear in the request line, headers, or body. Verify test_value does not appear in any subsequent Referer headers to third-party resources.

front.title: Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group (PEARG) Charter

section.name: Acknowledgments
section.t: WTX-1 was developed as part of the Nylo project to address the analytics gap created by the deprecation of third-party cookies, with a focus on privacy-respecting solutions for regulated industries including healthcare, finance, and government.

This document is positioned as a research contribution relevant to the IRTF Privacy Enhancements and Assessments Research Group (PEARG), whose charter includes "privacy analysis of proposed and deployed technologies." The authors welcome privacy analysis, critique, and discussion from the PEARG community.
